chapter.name: Motion in a Plane
chapter.blurb: The chapter introduces vectors as the language needed to describe motion in two dimensions: how they are added, subtracted, multiplied by numbers and resolved into components. It then defines position, displacement, velocity and acceleration in a plane and treats motion with constant acceleration as two independent straight-line motions. Projectile motion and uniform circular motion are worked out in detail as the two main applications.

scope_in.item: Distinguish scalars from vectors with examples, state how scalars are combined, and use the notation |A| = A for the magnitude of a vector

Describe position and displacement vectors, explain why displacement does not depend on the path and why its magnitude is less than or equal to the path length, and decide whether two vectors are equal
Find the magnitude and direction of a vector multiplied by a positive or negative real number, including a multiplier that carries a dimension
Add two vectors graphically by the head-to-tail (triangle) and parallelogram methods; use the commutative and associative laws; find the resultant of two perpendicular vectors (Example 3.1)
Describe the null vector and its properties, and subtract vectors using A - B = A + (-B)

Resolve a vector along two given directions and along the x- and y-axes using unit vectors i, j, k: Ax = A cos theta, Ay = A sin theta, A = sqrt(Ax^2 + Ay^2), tan theta = Ay/Ax; extend to three components
Add and subtract vectors by components (analytical method), and find the magnitude and direction of the resultant of two vectors from the law of cosines and the law of sines (Examples 3.2, 3.3)

Write position and displacement in component form; define average and instantaneous velocity and acceleration in a plane, find their components by differentiation, and state that velocity is tangential to the path (Example 3.4)
Use v = v0 + a t and r = r0 + v0 t + (1/2) a t^2 and their component forms for constant acceleration in a plane, treating the x and y motions independently (Example 3.5)
Analyse a projectile with air resistance neglected: components of velocity and position at time t, the parabolic equation of the path, and a body thrown horizontally from a height (Example 3.7)

Calculate the time to maximum height, time of flight, maximum height and horizontal range of a projectile, the maximum range at 45 degrees, and the equality of ranges for angles 45 + alpha and 45 - alpha (Examples 3.6, 3.8)

Explain why uniform circular motion is accelerated, state the direction and magnitude (v^2/R) of the centripetal acceleration, and relate angular speed, linear speed, time period and frequency (Example 3.9)
Apply all of the above to the chapter's exercises on path length and displacement, vector inequalities, projectiles and circular motion (Exercises 3.1-3.22)

concepts.name: Scalars, vectors and multiplication of a vector by a real number
concepts.description: What distinguishes a scalar from a vector, position and displacement vectors, equality of vectors, and the effect of multiplying a vector by a real number.
concepts.idea: A scalar is fixed by a number and a unit; a vector also needs a direction and adds by the triangle law.
concepts.rule: A scalar has magnitude only and is combined by ordinary algebra (scalars are added or subtracted only when they have the same units, but may be multiplied or divided with different units). A vector has magnitude and direction and obeys the triangle (or parallelogram) law of addition; its magnitude is written |A| = A. The position vector r of a point P is drawn from the origin O to P. The displacement vector from P to P' is the straight line from P to P' and does not depend on the path taken, so its magnitude is less than or equal to the path length. Two vectors are equal if and only if they have the same magnitude and the same direction; shifting a vector parallel to itself does not change it. Multiplying A by a positive number lambda gives a vector of magnitude lambda |A| in the direction of A; multiplying by a negative number -lambda gives a vector of magnitude lambda |A| in the opposite direction. If lambda has a dimension, lambda A has the product of the dimensions.
concepts.example: A displacement of 4 m due north multiplied by -2 is a displacement of 8 m due south.

A uniform solid cube of side 20 cm has a mass of 21.6 kg. Find its volume in m^3 and its density in kg/m^3, and state whether each of these two quantities is a scalar or a vector.
questions.a: Side = 20 cm = 0.2 m, so volume = (0.2 m)^3 = 0.008 m^3 (8 x 10^-3 m^3). Density = mass/volume = 21.6 kg/0.008 m^3 = 2700 kg/m^3. Both volume and density are scalars: each is specified completely by a number with its unit and has no direction.

questions.a: (a) Average speed = path length/time = 21 km/0.5 h = 42 km/h. (b) Magnitude of average velocity = magnitude of displacement/time = 12 km/0.5 h = 24 km/h. They are not equal: the average speed is larger because the path length is larger than the magnitude of the displacement.
s: Average speed = 21/0.5 = 42 km/h

questions.a: Turning left by 60 degrees after every equal side traces a regular hexagon of side 400 m. (a) After three sides he is at the vertex diametrically opposite the start; the displacement is the long diagonal of the hexagon = 2 x 400 = 800 m, while the path length is 3 x 400 = 1200 m. (b) After six sides he is back at the starting point, so the displacement is zero (a null vector) while the path length is 6 x 400 = 2400 m.
s: Track is a regular hexagon of side 400 m
Third turn: displacement 800 m, path length 1200 m
Sixth turn: displacement zero, path length 2400 m

questions.q: Vector A is a displacement of 12 m due east and B = -0.5A. A third vector C has the same magnitude as B but points due north. (i) Is C equal to B? (ii) Can C be obtained by multiplying A by some real number? Give a reason in each case.
questions.a: B has magnitude 0.5 x 12 = 6 m and points due west. (i) C is 6 m due north: it has the same magnitude as B but a different direction, so C is not equal to B, because equal vectors need the same magnitude and the same direction. (ii) No. Multiplying A by a positive number gives a vector due east and multiplying it by a negative number gives a vector due west; no real number can turn it towards the north.
s: B is 6 m due west; C differs from B in direction, so they are not equal
A real multiple of A lies only along east or west, so C cannot be obtained

questions.q: State, with a reason in each case, whether the following algebraic operations with physical quantities are meaningful: (a) adding any two scalars, (b) adding a scalar to a vector of the same dimensions, (c) multiplying any vector by any scalar.
questions.a: (a) Not always meaningful: two scalars can be added only if they represent quantities with the same units (a mass cannot be added to a temperature). (b) Not meaningful: a scalar has no direction and cannot be combined with a vector by the triangle law, even if the dimensions agree. (c) Meaningful: the product is a vector whose magnitude is scaled by the scalar and whose dimensions are the product of the two dimensions, for example a force multiplied by a time.
s: (a) Only scalars of the same units can be added
(b) A scalar cannot be added to a vector
(c) Any vector may be multiplied by any scalar, giving a vector

questions.q: Two displacement vectors are each 5 m long and point due east. One is drawn starting from the origin and the other starting from the point (2 m, 3 m). A student says they are different vectors because they are in different places. Evaluate this claim.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. Two vectors are equal if they have the same magnitude and the same direction, and these two do. Where a vector is drawn does not matter: a vector displaced parallel to itself is unchanged, so if one is slid parallel to itself until the tails coincide, the tips coincide as well.
s: Judgement - the two vectors are equal (same magnitude and same direction)
Reason - a vector shifted parallel to itself is unchanged, so its location does not enter the test of equality

questions.q: Make up a journey in a plane, with numbers of your own, between two points that can be reached by two different routes. Use it to show the difference between path length and displacement.
questions.a: Sample: P and Q are opposite corners of a rectangular field 30 m by 40 m. Route 1 goes along two sides: path length 30 + 40 = 70 m. Route 2 goes straight along the diagonal: path length 50 m. For both routes the displacement is the same vector, the straight line from P to Q of magnitude 50 m directed along the diagonal. So the displacement depends only on the end points, the path length depends on the route, and the path length is never less than the magnitude of the displacement (70 m > 50 m, and 50 m = 50 m for the straight route).
s: Two points and two different routes stated with their path lengths
Same displacement for both routes, with magnitude and direction given
Conclusion - path length depends on route and is greater than or equal to the magnitude of displacement

concepts.name: Addition and subtraction of vectors by the graphical method
concepts.description: Adding vectors by the head-to-tail (triangle) and parallelogram methods, the commutative and associative laws, the null vector and subtraction of vectors.
concepts.idea: Vectors are added by placing them head to tail; the resultant runs from the first tail to the last head.
concepts.rule: Head-to-tail (triangle) method: place the tail of B at the head of A; the resultant R = A + B is drawn from the tail of A to the head of B. Parallelogram method: bring the tails of A and B to a common origin O and complete the parallelogram; R is the diagonal drawn from O. The two methods are equivalent. Vector addition is commutative, A + B = B + A, and associative, (A + B) + C = A + (B + C). Two equal and opposite vectors add to the null vector 0, which has zero magnitude and no specifiable direction, with A + 0 = A, lambda 0 = 0 and 0 A = 0; the displacement of an object that returns to its starting point is a null vector. Subtraction is defined through addition: A - B = A + (-B). For two perpendicular vectors the magnitude of the resultant follows from the right-angled triangle they form. The magnitude of a resultant lies between the difference and the sum of the two magnitudes.
concepts.example: A walk of 9 m east followed by 12 m north is a single displacement of 15 m from the start, because the three vectors form a right-angled triangle.

Rain is falling vertically with a speed of 24 m/s. A wind starts blowing with a speed of 7 m/s from west to east. Find the magnitude of the resultant velocity of the rain and the tangent of the angle it makes with the vertical (to 2 significant figures). Towards which side should a person tilt an umbrella (that is, from which side does the rain now arrive)?
questions.a: The two velocities are perpendicular, so R = sqrt(24^2 + 7^2) = sqrt(625) = 25 m/s. If theta is the angle with the vertical, tan theta = 7/24 = 0.29. The rain now moves downward and towards the east, so it arrives from the west side: the umbrella must be tilted towards the west, at this angle with the vertical.

s: Draw -B and add it to A head to tail: A - B = A + (-B)

Find (a) the magnitude of the resultant velocity of the boat, (b) the tangent of the angle the resultant makes with the north direction, stating on which side of north it lies, and (c) the magnitude of the displacement of the boat in 30 minutes.
questions.a: (a) The two velocities are perpendicular, so R = sqrt(12^2 + 5^2) = sqrt(169) = 13 km/h. (b) If phi is the angle between R and north, tan phi = 5/12 (about 0.42); the resultant points to the east of north. (c) Displacement = resultant velocity x time = 13 km/h x 0.5 h = 6.5 km along the direction of R.
s: tan phi = 5/12, to the east of north
Displacement in 0.5 h = 6.5 km

questions.q: Three non-zero vectors satisfy a + b + c = 0. Explain (i) what figure they form when drawn head to tail, and (ii) why the magnitude of a can never be greater than the sum of the magnitudes of b and c.
questions.a: (i) A zero sum means that the head of the last vector lands on the tail of the first, so the three vectors drawn head to tail form a closed triangle (or lie along one line). (ii) From the relation, a = -(b + c), so |a| = |b + c|. One side of a triangle cannot be longer than the other two sides together, so |b + c| is at most |b| + |c|; hence |a| cannot exceed |b| + |c|.
s: Head to tail they form a closed triangle because the sum is zero
a = -(b + c), and |b + c| cannot exceed |b| + |c|

questions.q: For any two vectors a and b, establish geometrically that (a) |a + b| is less than or equal to |a| + |b|, and (b) |a + b| is greater than or equal to the difference between |a| and |b|. State when the equality sign holds in each case.
questions.a: Draw a and b head to tail; a + b is the third side of the triangle they form. (a) Any side of a triangle is shorter than the sum of the other two sides, so |a + b| < |a| + |b|; equality holds when the triangle collapses with a and b pointing in the same direction. (b) Any side of a triangle is longer than the difference of the other two sides, so |a + b| > the difference of |a| and |b|; equality holds when a and b point in opposite directions.
s: a, b and a + b form the sides of a triangle; a side is less than the sum of the other two
A side is greater than the difference of the other two
Equality: same direction for (a), opposite directions for (b)

questions.q: A student states: 'The resultant of two vectors is always larger in magnitude than either of the two vectors.' Evaluate this statement, giving an example.
questions.a: The statement is false. The magnitude of the resultant depends on the directions of the two vectors as well as on their magnitudes. For example, vectors of 5 units and 3 units pointing in opposite directions give a resultant of only 2 units, smaller than either. In general the magnitude of the resultant can be anything from the difference to the sum of the two magnitudes.
s: Judgement - false, with a valid counter-example
Reason - the resultant depends on the angle and ranges from the difference to the sum of the magnitudes

questions.q: Design a ruler-and-paper activity, using two displacement vectors of your own choice, to check that vector addition is commutative.
questions.a: Choose a scale, say 1 cm for 1 m, and two displacements, for example A = 5 m east and B = 3 m in a direction 60 degrees north of east. From a point O draw A, then draw B from the head of A; join O to the head of B to get A + B. Starting again from O, draw B first and then A from the head of B; join O to the final head to get B + A. Both constructions end at the same point, so the two resultants have the same length and direction (together the two constructions form a parallelogram with the resultant as the diagonal). Hence A + B = B + A.
s: Scale chosen and A then B drawn head to tail, resultant from the first tail to the last head
Second construction from the same point with B first and then A
Both resultants coincide in length and direction, so addition is commutative

concepts.name: Resolution of vectors: unit vectors and rectangular components
concepts.description: Resolving a vector along two given directions, unit vectors i, j and k, and the components of a vector along the axes of a rectangular coordinate system.
concepts.idea: Any vector in a plane can be written as the sum of two component vectors along chosen directions; along the x- and y-axes these are Ax i and Ay j.
concepts.rule: A vector A in a plane can be resolved along two non-zero vectors a and b of different directions in that plane: A = lambda a + mu b, with lambda and mu real numbers. A unit vector has magnitude 1, has no dimension and no unit, and only specifies a direction; i, j and k are the unit vectors along the x-, y- and z-axes and are perpendicular to each other. Any vector is A = |A| n, where n is the unit vector along A. In the x-y plane A = Ax i + Ay j with Ax = A cos theta and Ay = A sin theta, theta being the angle A makes with the x-axis. Ax and Ay are numbers (they can be positive, negative or zero), while Ax i and Ay j are vectors. Conversely A = sqrt(Ax^2 + Ay^2) and tan theta = Ay/Ax. In three dimensions Ax = A cos alpha, Ay = A cos beta, Az = A cos gamma and A = sqrt(Ax^2 + Ay^2 + Az^2); a position vector is r = x i + y j + z k.
concepts.example: A vector of magnitude 20 units at 30 degrees above the +x axis has Ax = 20 cos 30 = 17.3 units and Ay = 20 sin 30 = 10 units.

concepts.rule: If A = Ax i + Ay j and B = Bx i + By j, then R = A + B has Rx = Ax + Bx and Ry = Ay + By (and Rz = Az + Bz in three dimensions). For two vectors of magnitudes A and B with angle theta between them, the resultant has magnitude R = sqrt(A^2 + B^2 + 2AB cos theta) (the law of cosines). If R makes angle alpha with A and beta with B, then R/sin theta = A/sin beta = B/sin alpha (the law of sines), so sin alpha = (B/R) sin theta, and also tan alpha = B sin theta/(A + B cos theta).

concepts.name: Position, displacement, velocity and acceleration in a plane
concepts.description: Describing motion in two dimensions with the position vector, displacement, average and instantaneous velocity, and average and instantaneous acceleration in component form.
concepts.idea: In a plane, position, velocity and acceleration are vectors; velocity is tangent to the path and acceleration follows the change in velocity.
concepts.rule: Position vector r = x i + y j, where x and y are the coordinates of the object. Displacement from r to r' is delta r = r' - r = delta x i + delta y j. Average velocity = delta r/delta t, in the direction of delta r. The velocity v = dr/dt is the limit of the average velocity as delta t tends to zero; its direction is tangential to the path, in the direction of motion. In components vx = dx/dt, vy = dy/dt, v = sqrt(vx^2 + vy^2) and tan theta = vy/vx, theta being the angle with the x-axis. Average acceleration = delta v/delta t, in the direction of delta v; acceleration a = dv/dt with ax = dvx/dt and ay = dvy/dt. In one dimension the velocity and acceleration are always along the same line, but in two or three dimensions the angle between them may be anything from 0 to 180 degrees.
concepts.example: If r = 2t i + t^2 j (in metres, t in seconds), then v = 2i + 2t j m/s and a = 2j m/s^2.

concepts.name: Motion in a plane with constant acceleration and the equations of a projectile
concepts.description: The vector equations of motion for constant acceleration, their component form, the independence of the two perpendicular motions, and the position, velocity and path of a projectile.
concepts.idea: Motion in a plane with constant acceleration is two independent straight-line motions along perpendicular directions; a projectile has no horizontal acceleration and a downward acceleration g.
concepts.rule: For constant acceleration a: v = v0 + a t and r = r0 + v0 t + (1/2) a t^2. In components: vx = v0x + ax t, vy = v0y + ay t, x = x0 + v0x t + (1/2) ax t^2, y = y0 + v0y t + (1/2) ay t^2. The motions along x and y can be treated independently, as two separate simultaneous one-dimensional motions. A projectile is an object in flight after being thrown or projected. With air resistance neglected, x horizontal and y vertically upward, its acceleration is a = -g j (ax = 0, ay = -g). Launched from the origin with speed v0 at angle theta0 above the horizontal: v0x = v0 cos theta0, v0y = v0 sin theta0; x = (v0 cos theta0) t, y = (v0 sin theta0) t - (1/2) g t^2; vx = v0 cos theta0 (constant), vy = v0 sin theta0 - g t. Eliminating t gives the path y = (tan theta0) x - g x^2/(2 (v0 cos theta0)^2), which is of the form y = a x + b x^2, a parabola. At the highest point vy = 0.
concepts.example: A particle starts from the origin with v0 = 2i m/s and constant a = 3j m/s^2. At t = 2 s, v = 2i + 6j m/s and r = 4i + 6j m.

concepts.name: Time of flight, maximum height and horizontal range of a projectile
concepts.description: The time to reach the maximum height, the time of flight, the maximum height and the horizontal range of a projectile launched from level ground, and how the range depends on the angle of projection.
concepts.idea: The vertical motion fixes how long the projectile stays in flight and how high it rises; the horizontal motion during that time fixes the range.
concepts.rule: For a projectile launched with speed v0 at angle theta0 above the horizontal and returning to the launch level (air resistance neglected): time to reach the maximum height tm = v0 sin theta0/g (where vy = 0); time of flight Tf = 2 v0 sin theta0/g = 2 tm, from the symmetry of the parabolic path; maximum height hm = (v0 sin theta0)^2/(2g); horizontal range R = (v0 cos theta0) Tf = v0^2 sin 2theta0/g, the horizontal distance from the launch point to the point where the projectile passes y = 0 during its fall. For a given v0 the range is greatest when sin 2theta0 = 1, that is theta0 = 45 degrees, and the maximum range is Rm = v0^2/g. For elevations that exceed or fall short of 45 degrees by equal amounts the ranges are equal.
concepts.example: A ball launched at 10 m/s at 30 degrees above the horizontal with g = 10 m/s^2 (sin 30 = 0.5, sin 60 = 0.866) has tm = 0.5 s, Tf = 1 s, hm = 1.25 m and R = 100 x 0.866/10 = 8.66 m.

concepts.name: Uniform circular motion and centripetal acceleration
concepts.description: Motion in a circle at constant speed: the direction and magnitude of the centripetal acceleration, angular speed, time period and frequency, and the relations between them.
concepts.idea: An object moving in a circle at constant speed is accelerated because the direction of its velocity keeps changing; the acceleration points to the centre and has magnitude v^2/R.
concepts.rule: In uniform circular motion the speed is constant but the velocity, which is along the tangent, changes direction continuously, so the object is accelerated. The acceleration is directed towards the centre of the circle at every point (centripetal, meaning centre-seeking) and has magnitude ac = v^2/R. Its magnitude is constant but its direction keeps changing, so it is not a constant vector. Angular speed omega = (angle turned)/(time taken); v = R omega, so ac = omega^2 R. The time period T is the time for one revolution and the frequency nu = 1/T is the number of revolutions per second; v = 2 pi R/T = 2 pi R nu, omega = 2 pi nu and ac = 4 pi^2 nu^2 R.
concepts.example: An object moving at 4 m/s in a circle of radius 2 m has ac = 16/2 = 8 m/s^2 towards the centre and omega = 4/2 = 2 rad/s.

After one complete revolution the particle is back at the same point with the same velocity vector, so the change in velocity is zero and the average acceleration over the revolution is a null vector. s: Velocity vector is the same after one revolution, so change in velocity and hence average acceleration is a null vector
Instantaneous acceleration is never zero: v^2/R towards the centre at every instant

The instantaneous acceleration has magnitude v^2/R = (3.14)^2/1 = 9.86 m/s^2, so the average over a quarter revolution is smaller in magnitude than the instantaneous value.
s: Time for the quarter revolution = 0.5 s (quarter circumference/speed, or one quarter of T = 2 pi R/v)
Change in velocity = -3.14i - 3.14j m/s, magnitude 4.44 m/s
Average acceleration 8.88 m/s^2, less than v^2/R = 9.86 m/s^2

questions.a: The claim is wrong. The equation v = v0 + a t was obtained for an acceleration that is constant, and as a vector equation it cannot be used by simply adding magnitudes. In uniform circular motion the acceleration has constant magnitude but its direction keeps changing (always towards the centre), so it is not a constant vector. It changes only the direction of the velocity: the speed stays 5 m/s.
s: Judgement - wrong; the speed remains 5 m/s
Reason - centripetal acceleration is not a constant vector (direction changes), so the constant-acceleration equation does not apply; it only turns the velocity
